309.title: Grace and works
309.hook: Catholics and Lutherans agreed in 1999 that we're saved by grace, not by works, and good works follow
309.howItsDone: Christians across the churches describe good works, such as serving the poor, giving and caring for neighbors, as a grateful response to God's grace, and some churches mark Reformation Day on October 31 with joint Catholic–Lutheran prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was repentance, metanoia: pulling over and turning the car around. Your line was turn, and be forgiven.

Augsburg, Germany, 1999. In the city where Lutherans had once presented their confession of faith to the emperor, leaders of the Lutheran World Federation and of the Catholic Church sit down at one table and sign a document together. For centuries, the two churches had formally condemned each other's teaching on how a person is made right with God. Wars had been fought partly over it. Families split. Now they sign a statement saying: on the heart of this question, we agree. Not on everything. On the center. Today's word is what they agreed on.
screen: `AUGSBURG, 1999.` → `CENTURIES OF CONDEMNATION.` → `ON THE CENTER, WE AGREE.`

segments.voice: Justification is a courtroom word. To justify someone is to declare them in the right. In the Bible, the question is: how does a person come to be right with God? Paul's answer, in Ephesians, is the line from day two hundred eighty-nine: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God." And the very next lines go on: "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works." Grace first. Then good. But James says bluntly: "faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone." For centuries, Protestants and Catholics heard those texts pulling in different directions. Lutherans stressed that God declares sinners righteous, a free gift received by faith alone. Catholics stressed that God's grace truly makes a person righteous from within, and works through a changed life. Each suspected the other of missing something. The Joint Declaration put the shared center like this, in summary: by grace alone, through faith in what Christ has done, and not by anything people have earned, God accepts them and gives the Holy Spirit, who renews hearts and calls people to good works. Both sides agreed the old condemnations don't apply to the teaching as the other now presents it. They still describe some things differently, and some theologians on both sides objected. Since then, world bodies of Methodist, Anglican and Reformed churches have affirmed it too. The order fits in a pocket: grace comes first, and good works grow out of it, the way fruit grows on a tree that is already alive.
screen: `JUSTIFY: DECLARE IN THE RIGHT.` · `EPHESIANS 2, AND JAMES 2.` · `DECLARED RIGHT, OR MADE RIGHT?` · `1999: ON THE CENTER, AGREED.` · then, large: `CREATED IN CHRIST JESUS UNTO GOOD WORKS.`

segments.voice: Remember something you've been given that you didn't earn, and stay with it for a few breaths. Then, out of that thankfulness, not out of guilt or to prove anything, choose one small, specific good thing to do today: a call, a meal, a note, a chore done for someone else. If you pray, thank God for grace and offer the good work as thanks; if you don't, just let gratitude choose it.
Justification. Being made right with God. Catholics and Lutherans now agree: by grace, through faith, and good works follow.
Your line: grace first, then good. Thanks, not fear, does the choosing. Day three hundred nine, done.

310.title: The resurrection of the body
310.hook: not escape from the body, but bodies raised and made new
310.howItsDone: Christians say "the resurrection of the body" in the Apostles' Creed, and at funerals many churches pray in the hope of the resurrection, burying or committing the body with honor.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was justification, by grace through faith. Your line was grace first, then good.

Ask most people what Christians think happens after death, and you'll hear this: your soul floats out of your body to heaven, where it lives forever on a cloud, maybe with a harp. The body stays behind, like an old coat. Read the creed carefully, and it says something stranger, and more solid. Near the very end, just before life everlasting: I believe in the resurrection of the body. Not the escape of the soul. The body. Raised. Your hands, your face, your voice, somehow, made new.
screen: `A SOUL ON A CLOUD, WITH A HARP?` → `THE CREED SAYS SOMETHING ELSE.` → `THE BODY, RAISED.`

segments.voice: In the ancient world, plenty of thinkers taught that the body was a prison for the soul, and death was a release. Early Christians knew those ideas, and turned them down. Their hope was built on Easter. The risen Jesus wasn't a ghost. In Luke, he says: touch me and see, a spirit doesn't have flesh and bones. He eats a piece of fish in front of them. In John, he still carries the marks of the nails. And yet he's changed: he appears in locked rooms, and friends don't recognize him at first. Christians say what happened to Jesus is a first taste of what will happen to everyone. Paul's picture is a seed. You plant a bare seed, and up comes a whole plant, connected to the seed but far more glorious. "It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption." "It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body." A spiritual body isn't made of air. It's a body fully alive with God's Spirit, no longer dying. Paul admits there's a great deal we don't know about what that will be like. The Bible's last book pictures not souls leaving the earth, but a new heaven and a new earth, and God saying: "Behold, I make all things new." That's why Christians have cared so much for bodies: burying the dead with honor, running hospitals, feeding the hungry. Many churches now allow cremation too; the hope doesn't depend on what happens to the remains. If God will raise bodies, then bodies matter now: yours, and everyone else's.
screen: `NOT A PRISON FOR THE SOUL.` · `TOUCH ME AND SEE.` · `A SEED, AND WHAT GROWS FROM IT.` · `ALL THINGS NEW, SO BODIES MATTER NOW.` · then, large: `IT IS SOWN IN CORRUPTION; IT IS RAISED IN INCORRUPTION.`

segments.voice: Picture your body as Paul pictured it: a seed, not a shell you'll shed, with more in it than it looks, even the parts worn or scarred or aching, which Christians say are not thrown away. Then hold in mind, for a few breaths, someone else's body you love that is tired or ill or old. If you pray, give thanks to God for your body and theirs, and for the hope that both will be raised; if you don't, simply be grateful for them.

311.title: Life everlasting
311.hook: heaven, hell, purgatory: traditions differ, but all hope in God's mercy
311.howItsDone: Christians say "and the life everlasting" at the end of the Apostles' Creed, pray at funerals in the hope of eternal life, and Catholics, with some Anglicans and Lutherans, remember the dead on All Souls' Day, November 2.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was soma: the body, sown and raised. Your line was bodies matter.

Norwich, England, May 1373. A woman of thirty, her name unknown, is so sick her priest is called to her bedside. He holds a crucifix before her eyes. Over the next hours, she sees visions. She recovers, and later lives as an anchoress, walled into a small room beside the church of Saint Julian; tradition gives her its name: Julian of Norwich. In what she writes down, she asks God her hardest question: why sin, why so much pain? The answer she hears is still quoted today. She's the guide to today's word, the creed's last line.
screen: `NORWICH, MAY 1373.` → `A WOMAN NEAR DEATH.` → `HER HARDEST QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The creed ends: and the life everlasting. In John, the Greek is zoe aionios: the life of the age to come. It's not just more time, an endless Tuesday. It's a different kind of life, God's own life, which John says can begin now. John 3:16 is about it: "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life." After death? Here the churches honestly differ. They speak of heaven: being with God, seeing God face to face. Church teaching also speaks of hell: the real possibility of refusing God, and being separated from God. Some understand it as endless; some Christians hope that in the end even hell may be emptied, though that hope isn't the official teaching of the large churches. Fear of hell weighs on some people for years, sometimes even after they've stopped believing. If that's you, it's worth telling someone you trust, a pastor, a counselor or a doctor; and if you ever feel in danger, in the US you can call or text 988, or reach local emergency help. Catholics speak of purgatory: a purifying after death for those on their way to God. Orthodox Christians pray for the dead without defining purgatory, and Protestant churches generally don't hold it. But under all of it runs one hope: God's mercy. Julian heard it, in the old translation: "all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well." Revelation pictures the end alike: "God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death." That closes this part of the path: the creed, line by line, from I believe to life everlasting.

312.title: Not ashamed (Romans 1:1–17)
312.hook: Paul introduces himself to a church he's never met, and to the good news as power
312.howItsDone: Christians read Romans in church and in Bible studies, and some memorize Romans 1:16, "I am not ashamed of the gospel," as a statement of confidence in their faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was life everlasting, the creed's last line. Your line was mercy has the last word.

A letter to strangers is hard to write. You want them to know who you are, and to like you, but you also have something important to say. How do you start? Paul faces exactly that, writing to the Christians in Rome. He's never been there. He didn't found that church. He's heard about them, and they've heard about him, perhaps not all of it good. And this letter would go on to turn lives around: Augustine, Luther and Wesley each wrote about the part it played for them. A new part of the path begins here: Romans. Its first big claim is today's word.
screen: `A LETTER TO STRANGERS.` → `A CHURCH HE NEVER FOUNDED.` → `A LETTER THAT TURNED LIVES.`

segments.voice: Paul opens by telling them who he is: "Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, separated unto the gospel of God." Servant: the Greek word is doulos, a slave, someone who belongs to another. Then a warm greeting: "To all that be in Rome, beloved of God, called to be saints: Grace to you and peace." Saints, as on day three hundred seven: ordinary people, set apart. He says he longs to visit, so he can give them some spiritual gift. Then he catches himself and adds, in effect: I mean, so we can encourage each other. "that I may be comforted together with you by the mutual faith both of you and me." The great apostle, correcting himself mid-sentence so he won't sound like he's come to lecture. Then comes the line the whole letter stands on: "For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek." Why would anyone be ashamed? Because in Rome, a crucified man was the lowest thing imaginable. The cross was the empire's punishment for slaves and rebels. And Paul says: I'm not ashamed of it. It's power. The Greek word is dynamis, where we get dynamic. Then one more line, quoted from the prophet Habakkuk, the line Luther later said set him free: "The just shall live by faith."

Try Paul's way: say who you are, simply; greet them warmly; and let it be mutual, two people encouraging each other, not one giving and one receiving. If you pray, pray for that person by name, or by face; if you don't, just picture the hello, and let it be warm.

313.title: Everyone has gone astray (Romans 1:18–3:20)
313.hook: Paul argues that Jew and Gentile alike have missed the mark
313.howItsDone: Some Christians end the day with an examination of conscience: looking back over it, naming where they fell short, and asking God's forgiveness.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was not ashamed, from Paul's letter to strangers in Rome. Your line was someone who belongs to another.

A group chat, late in the evening. Someone starts listing everything wrong with everybody else. The coworker who never refills the coffee. The neighbor with the leaf blower at seven. Everyone piles on. Then one friend types a single line: you do that too. Silence. Paul does exactly this to his readers in Rome. Through the rest of his first chapter he describes a world that has turned away from God: greed, envy, gossip, cruelty, people who know better and don't care. You can almost hear the listeners nodding. Yes. Them. And then he turns around and points at the one nodding.
screen: `A LIST OF EVERYONE ELSE'S WRONGS.` → `THE LISTENERS NOD.` → `THEN PAUL TURNS AROUND.`

segments.voice: Here's the turn: "Therefore thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest: for wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself." The finger that was pointing out now points back. Paul builds his case in two halves. First, the nations who never had the law of Moses. They still had creation, he says: God's power can be seen in the things that are made. And they had a conscience, a law written on the heart, that sometimes accuses and sometimes excuses. Second, his own people, the Jewish people, who had the law and the promises. Paul is a Jew himself, arguing as an insider: having the law is a gift, he says, but hearing it isn't the same as keeping it. Then he lands it with a string of lines, mostly from the Psalms: "There is none righteous, no, not one." Nobody gets to stand on the balcony and look down. Paul's Greek word for sin is hamartia. Its verb, in older Greek, could mean to miss: a spear thrown that falls short of the target. So sin, for Paul, is not only a list of bad deeds. It's a condition everyone shares, a whole aim that's off. Christians describe how deep that goes in different ways, and those differences are coming in the days ahead. But the text is plain on one thing: Paul isn't sorting the world into good people and bad people. He's putting everyone in the same room. And that's where the good news can start.

314.title: But now (Romans 3:21–26)
314.hook: the hinge: all have sinned, and all are justified freely by grace
314.howItsDone: Christians often learn Romans 3:23–24 by heart; Protestant preaching returns to it again and again, and Catholic and Orthodox teaching reads it alongside baptism and a lifelong healing by grace.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was sin, hamartia, missing the mark. Your line was all of us.

A door weighs far more than its hinge, and the whole door swings on that small piece of metal. Paul's letter to the Romans has a hinge, two words long. For more than two chapters he has built a case like a courtroom closing argument. The nations without the law: guilty. His own people with the law: guilty too. Every mouth stopped, he says. The whole world stands in the dock, and the gavel is about to come down. Then, right where the verdict should be, Paul writes two little words, and the whole letter swings open.
screen: `A DOOR SWINGS ON A HINGE.` → `THE WHOLE WORLD IN THE DOCK.` → `THEN TWO LITTLE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here they are, in the King James Bible: "But now the righteousness of God without the law is manifested." But now. In Greek, nuni de. Everything before was the bad news, laid out carefully; everything after is the good news. And Paul doesn't take back a word of the bad news. He says it again: "For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God." Nobody is let off. But the very next line is just as wide: "Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus." The same all who fell short are the all who are offered grace. Three words to open. Justified comes from the courtroom: in Greek, being declared in the right, set right with the judge. Freely is the Greek word for a gift, something you don't pay for; John's Gospel uses it when Jesus says they hated him without a cause, for nothing. And grace, charis, is favor you didn't earn. Since the Reformation, Christians have argued about this passage. Protestants in Luther's line hear justified mainly as a verdict: God declares the guilty person righteous, a gift received by faith. Catholics and Orthodox Christians tend to stress that God's grace also makes a person righteous, healing and changing them over a lifetime. Remember the table in Augsburg from day three hundred nine: on the center, Lutherans and Catholics now say they agree. And the hinge is right there in the text. The story doesn't end at all have sinned. It turns on but now.

segments.voice: Bring to mind something that feels like a final verdict about you: a thing you did, a label you've carried, a sentence that begins I'm the kind of person who. 315.title: Abraham believed (Romans 4)
315.hook: Abraham trusted God and it was counted as righteousness
315.howItsDone: Christians often point to Abraham as the model of faith, and many pray by naming a specific worry and entrusting it to God, sometimes with the words of a psalm.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was but now, nuni de, the hinge of Romans. Your line was the story keeps going.

An old man stands outside his tent at night. He's well past seventy-five. His wife Sarah is old too, long past childbearing. They have no children, and by every sensible measure never will. And God takes him outside and says: look up, count the stars if you can. So shall your descendants be. Centuries later, in the middle of his big argument about grace, Paul needs one example everyone in Rome respects, Jew and Gentile alike. He doesn't pick a king or a prophet. He goes back to that old man under the stars.
screen: `AN OLD MAN UNDER THE STARS.` → `COUNT THEM, IF YOU CAN.` → `PAUL GOES BACK TO ABRAHAM.`

segments.voice: Paul quotes Genesis, in the King James Bible: "Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness." Believed: the Greek verb shares a root with pistis, faith, and means trust more than opinion. Abraham didn't agree to a list of ideas; he leaned his whole weight on a promise. Counted is an accountant's word in Greek: credited, entered in the ledger as being in the right with God. Timing matters too. In Genesis, this verse comes before Abraham is circumcised, before the covenant sign. So, Paul says, Abraham is the father of everyone who trusts like this: his own people, and the nations too. Abraham looked honestly at his own body, as good as dead at about a hundred, and at Sarah's, and still trusted. "Who against hope believed in hope." Genesis is honest too: Abraham and Sarah both laugh at the promise at different moments, and they try a plan of their own along the way. Faith here is not the absence of doubt. It's trusting anyway. Christians read this chapter alongside the letter of James, which also points to Abraham and says faith without works is dead. How the two fit has been argued over, sharply at the Reformation. Many Protestants today hear them as two sides of one coin; Catholic and Orthodox teaching stresses that faith and works belong together. Jews and Muslims also honor Abraham as a father of faith. After a week of big words, grace, sin, but now, it comes down to one old man, looking up, trusting.
screen: `PISTIS: TRUST, NOT OPINION.` · `COUNTED: CREDITED TO HIS ACCOUNT.` · `BEFORE THE SIGN, FATHER OF ALL.` · `AGAINST HOPE, BELIEVED IN HOPE.` · then, large: `ABRAHAM BELIEVED GOD.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you're gripping tightly right now, a test result, a child far away, money, a decision you keep replaying, and hold it in your mind like something in your fist. Look at it honestly, the way Abraham looked at his own old body, then slowly open your hand. If you pray, hand that one thing to God and leave it there; if you don't, simply loosen your grip for two minutes and notice what happens in your chest.
Faith. Pistis in Greek: trust, leaning your weight on a promise. Abraham's was counted to him as righteousness.
